HHS Student Intern (Administrative) 2026 — Pathways Internship Program

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is accepting applications for its Student Intern (Administrative) position through the U.S. federal government’s Pathways Internship Program.

This opportunity gives eligible students the chance to gain practical experience within the U.S. federal government while receiving on-the-job training and developmental assignments in administrative support, program support, organizational management, reporting, meeting coordination, stakeholder engagement, and other government-related functions.

The position is located within the Office of the Secretary of Health and Human Services, under the Assistant Secretary for Administration, and the announcement may be used to fill multiple positions in different locations across the United States.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to students interested in public administration, government, business administration, project management, program management, organizational management, policy, executive support, and administrative careers.

However, applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements because U.S. citizenship is required for this position.

HHS Student Internship 2026: Key Details

  • Opportunity: Student Intern (Administrative)
  • Organization: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
  • Office: Office of the Secretary of Health and Human Services
  • Administrative Office: Assistant Secretary for Administration
  • Program: Pathways Internship Program
  • Opportunity Type: Internship
  • Job Series: 0399 – Administration and Office Support Student Trainee
  • Grade: GS-4 to GS-5
  • Salary: $31,103–$45,239 per year
  • Work Schedule: Full-time
  • Work Arrangement: Telework eligible, depending on agency policy
  • Remote: No
  • Travel: Not required
  • Appointment: Internship, not-to-exceed 13 months
  • Promotion Potential: GS-5
  • Federal Service: Excepted Service
  • Drug Test: No
  • Background Investigation: Suitability/Fitness
  • Deadline: August 14, 2026, or earlier if the applicant limit is reached

About the HHS Student Intern Administrative Position

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is offering Student Trainee positions under the federal government’s Pathways Internship Program.

The position is classified under occupational series 0399 — Administration and Office Support Student Trainee.

The purpose of the position is to provide students with practical, developmental work experience while they continue their education.

Interns will receive on-the-job training and may be assigned responsibilities designed to help them develop professional skills while supporting HHS programs and administrative operations.

The position is based within the Office of the Secretary of Health and Human Services, specifically under the Assistant Secretary for Administration.

The announcement may be used to fill multiple vacancies across several locations.

The internship appointment is currently listed as not-to-exceed 13 months. Managers may have the option to extend appointments on a case-by-case basis, although extensions are not guaranteed.

What Will HHS Student Interns Do?

The position involves both administrative support and program support responsibilities.

The duties are designed to provide students with practical exposure to how a major federal government department operates.

1. Administrative Support Duties

Administrative duties may include:

  • Receiving and recording administrative documents.
  • Planning meetings.
  • Scheduling meetings.
  • Coordinating meetings.
  • Compiling information for reports.
  • Compiling information for metrics.
  • Supporting program updates.
  • Performing administrative and technical duties.
  • Supporting administrative services.
  • Assisting with organizational management activities.

Through these responsibilities, interns may develop practical experience in areas such as:

  • Calendar and schedule management.
  • Meeting coordination.
  • Documentation.
  • Reporting.
  • Information management.
  • Administrative operations.
  • Organizational management.
  • Communication with stakeholders.
  • Office coordination.

These skills are transferable to a wide range of careers in government, business, project management, administration, and organizational operations.

2. Program Support Duties

Interns may also assist with program-related activities.

These responsibilities may include:

  • Working with management.
  • Working with stakeholders.
  • Supporting the development of new systems.
  • Assisting with implementation of systems.
  • Supporting implementation of programs.
  • Preparing reports.
  • Preparing position papers.
  • Preparing briefing materials.
  • Preparing talking points.
  • Preparing presentations for senior leadership.

This area of the internship can be particularly valuable for students interested in program management, public policy, government operations, project management, organizational development, and leadership support.

Benefits of the HHS Student Internship

The HHS Student Intern position offers students the opportunity to gain experience in a major U.S. federal government department.

Gain Federal Government Experience

Interns can gain direct exposure to federal government operations and learn how administrative and program-support functions contribute to organizational performance.

Having government experience can be valuable for students interested in public-sector careers and other professions that involve government institutions.

Develop Professional Skills

The internship provides practical opportunities to develop skills in:

  • Administration.
  • Organization.
  • Communication.
  • Meeting coordination.
  • Scheduling.
  • Reporting.
  • Program support.
  • Stakeholder coordination.
  • Presentation preparation.
  • Information management.
  • Organizational management.

Gain Experience Supporting Leadership

Interns may contribute to reports, briefing materials, presentations, talking points, and other materials prepared for senior leadership.

This can help students understand how information is organized and presented to decision-makers.

Receive On-the-Job Training

The position is designed around developmental assignments and on-the-job training.

Students can therefore gain practical experience while continuing to develop their academic and professional knowledge.

Potential Pathway to Future Federal Employment

One of the most attractive features of the Pathways Internship Program is the possibility of conversion.

Eligible interns may potentially be converted to a permanent or term position within HHS after successfully completing the required internship program requirements.

However, conversion is not guaranteed.

Conversion depends on factors including:

  • Available funding.
  • Organizational needs.
  • Student performance.
  • Educational completion.
  • Training requirements.
  • Availability of an appropriate position.
  • Meeting applicable qualification standards.

Salary and Employment Conditions

The advertised salary range for the position is:

$31,103 to $45,239 per year

The actual salary will be adjusted based on the duty location.

The position is classified at the GS-4 through GS-5 level.

The position is:

  • Full-time.
  • Non-supervisory.
  • Not a research position.
  • Not represented by a union.
  • Not subject to a drug test.
  • In the Excepted Service.
  • Subject to a suitability/fitness background investigation.

The position is telework eligible, depending on agency policy, but it is not classified as a fully remote position.

Travel is not required.

Relocation expenses are not reimbursed.

Available Locations

The announcement indicates that vacancies may be available in multiple locations.

These include:

  • Denver, Colorado
  • Washington, District of Columbia
  • Atlanta, Georgia
  • Chicago, Illinois
  • Kansas City, Kansas
  • Boston, Massachusetts
  • Dallas County, Texas
  • Location negotiable after selection

Although the position is associated with the Office of the Secretary in Washington, D.C., the announcement can be used to fill positions in several locations.

Who Is Eligible for the HHS Student Internship?

The opportunity is specifically intended for students.

Applicants must be:

  • Currently enrolled in a qualifying educational institution; or
  • Accepted for enrollment in a qualifying educational institution.

Applicants must also be pursuing a qualifying:

  • Degree.
  • Diploma.
  • Certificate.
  • Educational credential.

Students may be enrolled on either a full-time or part-time basis, provided they meet the applicable Pathways requirements.

Eligible Educational Institutions

The announcement recognizes a broad range of educational institutions.

These may include:

  • Four-year colleges and universities.
  • Community colleges.
  • Junior colleges.
  • Professional schools.
  • Technical schools.
  • Vocational schools.
  • Trade schools.
  • Graduate institutions.
  • Other qualifying educational institutions.

The educational institution must meet the applicable accreditation requirements.

Academic Requirements

Applicants must be in good academic standing.

The announcement establishes different GPA requirements depending on the educational program.

Undergraduate Students

Students pursuing an undergraduate degree must have a minimum cumulative GPA of:

2.5

Professional Master’s Students

Students enrolled in a professional master’s degree program must have a minimum GPA of:

3.0

Applicants must be able to provide documentation demonstrating their student status.

Educational Requirements for GS-4

For the GS-4 level, applicants must have completed:

Two academic years of post-high-school education leading toward an associate’s degree.

Educational Requirements for GS-5

For the GS-5 level, applicants must have completed:

Four academic years of post-high-school education leading toward a bachelor’s degree or equivalent degree.

The announcement also states that applications may be accepted from students who expect to complete qualifying education within nine months from the date of application, subject to the agency’s requirements.

U.S. Citizenship Requirement

One of the most important eligibility conditions is that:

U.S. citizenship is required.

This means applicants should not assume that being an international student, studying in the United States, or having a foreign degree automatically makes them eligible.

Applicants must satisfy the citizenship requirement as well as all other eligibility conditions.

Can Applicants from Ghana or Other Countries Apply?

Based on the announcement provided, non-U.S. citizens do not meet the stated citizenship requirement.

Therefore, applicants from Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Uganda, India, the United Kingdom, Canada, and other countries would not qualify if they are not U.S. citizens.

The opportunity is therefore primarily relevant to U.S. citizens who meet the student and academic requirements.

Foreign Education Requirements

Applicants who are relying on education completed at a foreign college or university must provide evidence showing that their education is equivalent to education obtained through an accredited U.S. educational institution.

The announcement requires foreign education to be evaluated by an accredited private organization specializing in the interpretation of foreign education programs.

The evaluation must establish U.S. educational equivalency and include a course-by-course listing.

Applicants relying on foreign education should ensure that the required evaluation documentation is available when applying.

Failure to provide the necessary documentation may result in loss of consideration.

Required Application Documents

Submitting only a resume is not a complete application.

Applicants must submit the full application package and all required supporting documents.

Federal Resume

The resume must:

  • Not exceed two pages.
  • Clearly describe duties.
  • Include accomplishments.
  • Highlight relevant skills.
  • Include start and end dates.
  • Provide sufficient information to demonstrate qualifications.

The announcement encourages applicants to use the USAJOBS Resume Builder.

Online Application

Applicants must complete the online occupational questionnaire and submit their answers.

Proof of Student Status

Applicants must provide documentation demonstrating that they are currently enrolled or have been accepted for enrollment in a qualifying educational program.

Transcripts

Copies of transcripts are acceptable at the application stage, although official transcripts may be requested if an applicant is selected.

Additional documentation may be required for applicants applying under special eligibility categories, such as certain veterans, military spouses, federal employees, or other special appointment authorities.

How to Prepare a Strong Federal Resume

Applicants should understand that a federal resume is different from many traditional private-sector resumes.

The announcement specifically states that applicants must provide enough information for the agency to determine whether they meet the qualifications.

Your resume should clearly identify:

  • Position title.
  • Employer.
  • Beginning date.
  • Ending date.
  • Hours worked per week where applicable.
  • Duties performed.
  • Accomplishments.
  • Relevant skills.
  • Experience related to the position.

Applicants should avoid simply copying the duties from the job announcement into their resumes.

Instead, demonstrate how your own experience relates to the position.

For example, if you have experience coordinating meetings, managing calendars, preparing reports, supporting executives, organizing events, maintaining records, communicating with stakeholders, or preparing presentations, describe those activities clearly and specifically.

Volunteer Experience May Count

Another important point is that qualifying experience does not necessarily have to come from traditional paid employment.

The announcement states that qualifying experience may include both paid and unpaid experience.

This can include volunteer work completed through:

  • National service programs.
  • Professional organizations.
  • Philanthropic organizations.
  • Community organizations.
  • Student organizations.
  • Social organizations.
  • Other organizations.

This is particularly useful for students who may have limited formal employment experience.

Volunteer activities that demonstrate leadership, administration, organization, communication, project coordination, or program support may help demonstrate relevant experience.

Background Investigation and Suitability

Selected applicants will be subject to a background security investigation and favorable adjudication.

The position is classified as:

Non-Sensitive / Low Risk

Applicants should ensure that all information provided in the application is accurate.

The federal government may verify information concerning:

  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Eligibility.
  • Other information included in the application.

Applicants should therefore avoid submitting inaccurate or misleading information.

USA Hire Assessments

Some applicants may be required to complete USA Hire competency-based assessments after submitting their application.

If an assessment is required, applicants will receive instructions through the application process and/or email.

Applicants should:

  1. Access the assessment using the unique link provided.
  2. Review all instructions before starting.
  3. Complete the assessment within the stated deadline.
  4. Allow sufficient time to complete the assessment.

The announcement recommends setting aside at least three hours, although many applicants may complete the assessments in less time.

If an applicant receives an assessment link after the announcement has closed, they may be required to complete the assessment within 48 hours of receiving the link.

Reasonable Accommodation for USA Hire Assessments

Applicants with a disability covered by the Rehabilitation Act who believe that the disability could interfere with completing the USA Hire assessments may request reasonable accommodation.

Requests should be made before beginning the assessments.

Applicants may need to provide appropriate supporting documentation as part of the accommodation process.

Important Application Deadline

The application period opened on:

August 10, 2026

The stated deadline is:

August 14, 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern Time

However, applicants should apply as early as possible.

The announcement states that it may close before the stated deadline if the applicant limit is reached.

There is also an inconsistency within the announcement regarding the applicant limit. The overview states that the announcement will close after 300 applications, while the additional-information section says it is anticipated to close when the 50th application is received or at 11:59 PM on August 14, 2026, whichever comes first.

Because of this discrepancy, applicants should not wait until the final day.

How to Apply for the HHS Student Internship

Applicants must apply through USAJOBS.

The general application process involves:

Step 1: Create or Log Into USAJOBS

Applicants must have a USAJOBS account.

Step 2: Select Your Resume

Select an appropriate federal resume from your USAJOBS account.

Step 3: Upload Supporting Documents

Upload proof of student status, transcripts, and any other documents required for your circumstances.

Step 4: Complete the Occupational Questionnaire

Applicants must answer the online application questions.

Step 5: Review Your Application

Carefully review all information before submitting.

Make sure your education, employment dates, experience, and eligibility information are accurate.

Step 6: Submit the Application

Click the appropriate submission button and ensure that the application is successfully submitted.

Step 7: Complete USA Hire Assessments

If required, complete the USA Hire assessments within the specified timeframe.

Step 8: Monitor Your Application

Applicants can log into their USAJOBS account to monitor the status of their application and review correspondence from the agency.

APPLY HERE

Selection Process

After applications are submitted, HHS will review resumes and supporting documentation to determine whether applicants meet the minimum qualifications.

Eligible and qualified candidates may be referred to hiring managers.

Interviews may also be conducted.

The agency expects to make a selection within approximately 45 days after the closing date.

Applicants should therefore regularly check:

  • Their email.
  • Their USAJOBS account.
  • Their application status.
  • Any assessment notifications.

For more information about this application visit HERE

More global internship programs visit the OFY Website HERE

Is Previous Work Experience Required?

The announcement focuses heavily on educational and student eligibility requirements rather than requiring a specific number of years of professional experience.

However, relevant experience can strengthen an application.

Experience in areas such as:

  • Administration.
  • Office support.
  • Project coordination.
  • Event coordination.
  • Scheduling.
  • Reporting.
  • Communication.
  • Program support.
  • Research.
  • Data compilation.
  • Stakeholder coordination.
  • Executive support.

may be useful when demonstrating suitability for the role.

Both paid and qualifying unpaid experience may be considered.

Can This Internship Lead to a Permanent Federal Government Job?

Potentially, yes.

The Pathways Internship Program provides a potential route toward federal employment.

Interns may be eligible for non-competitive conversion to a permanent or term federal position after completing the applicable requirements.

To be considered for conversion, interns must generally:

  • Complete at least 480 hours of internship work experience.
  • Complete the required degree.
  • Meet the qualification standards for the position.
  • Meet agency-specific requirements.
  • Successfully perform their duties.
  • Complete required training and development requirements.

However, conversion is not guaranteed.

Factors such as funding, organizational needs, job availability, student performance, and education can affect whether conversion occurs.

Why Students Should Consider This Opportunity

The HHS Student Intern position can provide an excellent foundation for students interested in government and administrative careers.

It combines:

  • Practical government experience.
  • Professional development.
  • On-the-job training.
  • Administrative experience.
  • Program-support experience.
  • Exposure to senior leadership.
  • Potential federal career opportunities.

Students can use the experience to strengthen their future applications for government, nonprofit, consulting, business, project management, and administrative positions.

Important Applicant Checklist

Before applying, make sure you can answer “Yes” to the following:

  • Are you a U.S. citizen?
  • Are you currently enrolled or accepted for enrollment?
  • Are you pursuing a qualifying degree, diploma, or certificate?
  • Are you in good academic standing?
  • Do you meet the minimum GPA requirement?
  • Do you meet the education requirements for the applicable grade level?
  • Can you provide proof of student status?
  • Can you provide transcripts if requested?
  • Does your federal resume contain complete employment dates?
  • Does your resume clearly describe your duties and accomplishments?
  • Is your resume no more than two pages?
  • Can you satisfy the required background investigation?
  • Are you prepared to complete USA Hire assessments if required?
  • Can you submit your application before the position closes?

Pro Tip for Applicants

Federal government applications are different from ordinary private-sector job applications.

Do not submit a generic resume and expect the hiring team to infer your qualifications.

Instead, clearly document your relevant experience, responsibilities, accomplishments, dates, hours worked, education, and skills.

For example, rather than simply stating “excellent organizational skills,” explain how you used those skills to coordinate meetings, manage schedules, prepare reports, maintain records, support senior officials, organize events, compile information, or coordinate stakeholders.

Most importantly, apply as early as possible.

Because the announcement may close once the applicant limit is reached, waiting until August 14 could mean missing the opportunity even if the official deadline has not yet passed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this an internship or a job?

It is a Student Intern/Student Trainee internship under the federal government’s Pathways Internship Program.

Is the internship full-time?

Yes. The position is advertised as full-time.

Is the position remote?

No. It is not classified as a remote position, although it is telework eligible depending on agency policy.

How much does the internship pay?

The salary range is $31,103 to $45,239 per year, depending on duty location.

Can international students apply?

The announcement states that U.S. citizenship is required. Therefore, non-U.S. citizens do not meet the stated citizenship requirement.

Can applicants from Ghana apply?

Applicants from Ghana can only qualify if they meet the U.S. citizenship requirement and all other eligibility conditions. Ghanaian citizens who are not U.S. citizens do not meet the stated citizenship requirement.

What is the minimum GPA?

The minimum GPA is 2.5 for undergraduate degree programs and 3.0 for professional master’s degree programs.

Do I need previous professional experience?

The announcement does not establish a traditional minimum number of years of professional experience. However, relevant paid, unpaid, volunteer, academic, or organizational experience may strengthen your application.

Can volunteer experience count?

Yes. The announcement states that qualifying experience may include paid and unpaid experience, including volunteer work.

Can this internship lead to a permanent federal position?

Potentially. Eligible interns may qualify for non-competitive conversion after satisfying the applicable Pathways requirements. However, conversion is not guaranteed.

When is the application deadline?

The stated deadline is August 14, 2026, at 11:59 PM Eastern Time. However, the announcement may close earlier if the applicant limit is reached.

Conclusion

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Student Intern (Administrative) opportunity offers eligible students an opportunity to gain practical experience within the U.S. federal government through the Pathways Internship Program.

Successful interns can develop valuable skills in administrative support, program support, scheduling, meeting coordination, reporting, organizational management, stakeholder engagement, presentation preparation, and senior leadership support.

The position also offers a competitive salary range of $31,103 to $45,239 per year, depending on location, and may provide a potential pathway toward future federal employment after successful completion of the Pathways requirements.

However, applicants must carefully review the eligibility criteria. U.S. citizenship is required, applicants must be enrolled or accepted for enrollment in a qualifying educational program, and they must meet the relevant GPA and education requirements.

The application deadline is August 14, 2026, but because the announcement may close early after reaching its applicant limit, eligible candidates should submit their applications as soon as possible.

item.content:encoded:
The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) is offering an opportunity for individuals interested in graduate professional development, program management, higher education administration, student services, and career development through its Graduate Student Professional Development Program Management Intern position.

This internship is based within MIT’s Career Advising & Professional Development (CAPD) – Graduate Student Professional Development area and provides an opportunity to contribute to programs designed to help graduate students build professional competencies and prepare for diverse career pathways.

The role combines program administration, project coordination, participant communication, admissions support, event coordination, data tracking, reporting, and professional development programming. It could therefore be particularly relevant to candidates who want to build practical experience in program management and higher education administration.

For professionals seeking to strengthen their project and program coordination experience, the position offers exposure to a highly structured academic environment and the opportunity to work with a diverse, multinational community.

About the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) is a globally recognized research university located in Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States.

MIT is known for its work across science, technology, engineering, mathematics, business, economics, social sciences, and other academic and professional disciplines. The Institute also places significant emphasis on innovation, research, interdisciplinary collaboration, and preparing students for professional careers.

Working at MIT can provide exposure to an international academic and professional environment, and the university emphasizes collaboration, inclusion, professional development, and employee support.

For this particular position, the successful candidate would work within the Career Advising & Professional Development function, supporting programs designed to help MIT graduate students develop skills and competencies relevant to their future careers.

About the Graduate Student Professional Development Program Management Internship

The Graduate Student Professional Development Program Management Intern position is located within Career Advising & Professional Development’s Graduate Student Professional Development team.

The team helps graduate students build professional competencies and supports the expansion of graduate professional-development programming.

The intern will contribute to the administration and delivery of certificate programs and other professional development activities. This includes supporting the complete program lifecycle, from applications and admissions through participation, progress tracking, completion, assessment, and reporting.

The position therefore combines several areas, including:

  • Program management
  • Project coordination
  • Higher education administration
  • Student and participant services
  • Admissions administration
  • Event coordination
  • Stakeholder communication
  • Data collection and tracking
  • Program assessment
  • Reporting
  • Professional development programming
  • Written and visual communications
  • Administrative operations

This makes the opportunity particularly interesting for candidates who want to develop a career in project management, program management, education administration, career services, student affairs, or organizational operations.

Key Responsibilities

1. Manage Certificate Program Application Cycles

One of the major responsibilities will involve supporting the administration of certificate program application cycles.

This may include helping manage applications as they are received, ensuring that information is organized properly, supporting the admissions process, and helping ensure that applicants move through the appropriate stages of the program.

The intern may therefore gain practical experience with:

  • Application management
  • Candidate communication
  • Admissions coordination
  • Evaluation processes
  • Applicant tracking
  • Program administration
  • Deadline management

This experience can be highly transferable to other program management and administrative roles.

2. Coordinate Admissions and Applicant Processes

The position involves helping coordinate admissions for professional development programs.

The intern will assist with processes related to:

  • Applicant evaluation
  • Admissions decisions
  • Acceptances
  • Waitlists
  • Applicant inquiries
  • Communication with prospective participants

The role also requires the candidate to respond promptly to applicant questions.

Strong communication skills will therefore be important because the intern may interact with individuals at different stages of the application and admissions process.

3. Support Evaluation and Selection Processes

The intern will also help calibrate evaluation processes for consistency.

This responsibility suggests that the candidate may participate in administrative activities designed to ensure that applications or candidates are evaluated according to consistent standards.

Attention to detail will be particularly important here.

Applicants should be comfortable working with structured processes, reviewing information carefully, maintaining accurate records, and ensuring that administrative procedures are followed consistently.

4. Coordinate Certificate Program Sessions

Another significant part of the position involves coordinating the logistics associated with certificate program sessions.

This may involve working with:

  • Speakers
  • Facilitators
  • Participants
  • Campus support teams
  • Administrative contacts
  • Other program stakeholders

The intern will help coordinate practical requirements surrounding program sessions, ensuring that activities run smoothly.

This could include logistical coordination related to speakers and facilitators, including arrangements involving payment, travel, and campus support.

Candidates with experience in event management, travel coordination, scheduling, meeting coordination, or executive and administrative support may therefore have useful transferable experience.

5. Track Participant Progress

The role also involves monitoring participant progress throughout the program.

The intern will help track participants as they move toward completing their certificate requirements.

This could require maintaining accurate records, monitoring completion milestones, identifying outstanding requirements, and supporting communication with participants.

The position therefore requires strong organizational skills and attention to detail.

Experience with spreadsheets, databases, tracking systems, project management tools, or administrative records can be beneficial.

6. Support Certificate Completion and Presentations

The intern will also contribute to activities associated with certificate completion, including certificate presentation.

This means the role does not stop once participants are admitted.

Instead, the intern supports the program throughout its lifecycle:

Application → Evaluation → Admission → Participation → Progress Tracking → Completion → Certificate Presentation

This provides valuable exposure to end-to-end program administration.

7. Assist With Program Assessment

Program assessment is another important component of the internship.

The intern will support efforts to evaluate professional development programs and determine how effectively they are serving participants.

This may involve assisting with:

  • Data collection
  • Program evaluation
  • Participant information
  • Feedback
  • Performance tracking
  • Reporting
  • Program improvement activities

Candidates interested in data analysis, monitoring and evaluation, business analysis, project management, or program management may find this aspect particularly useful.

8. Data Collection and Reporting

The position also involves supporting data collection and reporting.

Accurate data can help the Graduate Student Professional Development team understand participation, program completion, and other relevant outcomes.

The intern may therefore gain experience working with administrative data and turning program information into useful reports.

Strong attention to detail will be important because inaccurate data can affect program reporting and decision-making.

9. Create Written and Visual Communications

Communication is another major component of the position.

The intern will create written and visual communications for:

  • Graduate students
  • Faculty
  • Staff
  • Program participants
  • Other members of the MIT community

This means candidates should be comfortable communicating information clearly across different platforms.

Experience with professional writing, presentations, digital communication, newsletters, social media, graphic communication, or other forms of content development may be useful.

10. Support Graduate Professional Development Events

Beyond certificate programs, the intern will also support broader graduate professional development events.

This provides additional exposure to event and program coordination.

Responsibilities may involve helping with:

  • Event logistics
  • Scheduling
  • Participant communication
  • Speaker coordination
  • Administrative preparation
  • Follow-up activities
  • Event-related communications

Candidates who have previously supported conferences, workshops, seminars, training programs, career events, or institutional events may have relevant transferable experience.

11. Contribute Ideas for Program Growth

MIT is also looking for someone who can contribute ideas for the growth and improvement of its programs.

This means the internship is not necessarily limited to following existing administrative procedures.

The successful candidate may have opportunities to identify improvements, suggest new ideas, and contribute to the development of graduate professional development programming.

Creative thinking, initiative, problem-solving, and an understanding of participant needs can therefore be valuable.

12. Work With a Diverse and Multinational Community

MIT specifically highlights the importance of applying culturally responsive practices when serving its diverse, multinational community.

The successful candidate will therefore need to work effectively with people from different backgrounds, cultures, experiences, and perspectives.

The position also emphasizes fostering an inclusive work environment.

Strong interpersonal skills, cultural awareness, professionalism, respect, and adaptability will therefore be important qualities.

Required Qualifications

According to the MIT posting, applicants must meet several core requirements.

Bachelor’s Degree

A Bachelor’s degree is required.

The specific field of study is not stated in the job description provided.

Therefore, candidates from a range of academic backgrounds may potentially qualify, provided they also meet the other requirements.

Program Support Experience

Applicants must have program support experience.

This is an important requirement.

Relevant experience could potentially include supporting:

  • Academic programs
  • Training programs
  • Professional development programs
  • Conferences
  • Workshops
  • Student programs
  • Administrative programs
  • Community initiatives
  • Events
  • Recruitment programs
  • Organizational projects

Candidates should emphasize the program coordination and administrative aspects of their previous experience when preparing an application.

Skills and Competencies Required

MIT is looking for candidates with strong organizational and interpersonal capabilities.

Strong Organizational Skills

The position involves managing applications, admissions, communications, events, participant progress, data, and reporting.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are open for the Climate Education and Community Engagement online course offered by the Cornell Civic Ecology Lab at Cornell University.

The four-week global course is designed for educators, students, community leaders, NGO professionals, volunteers, parents and other individuals interested in connecting climate knowledge with practical education and community action.

The course will run online from September 8 to October 4, 2026. Participants who complete the weekly course requirements and final project will receive a Cornell University PDF certificate documenting 25 professional development hours.

No previous background in climate science is required, and participants from all countries can register. Tiered tuition is available, with a reduced fee for residents of lower-cost countries and a limited number of competitive need-based scholarships.

The deadline to apply for scholarship support is September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Climate Education and Community Engagement Course: Key Information

Item Details
Course title Climate Education and Community Engagement
Abbreviation CECE
Provider Cornell Civic Ecology Lab
Institution Cornell University
Course dates September 8–October 4, 2026
Duration Four weeks
Format Online and primarily asynchronous
Weekly workload Approximately four to five hours
Live component Optional live webinar or discussion session
Learning platforms edX Edge and Zoom
Certificate Cornell University PDF certificate
Professional development hours 25 hours
Standard fee $90
Reduced fee $20
Scholarship availability Limited, competitive and need-based
Scholarship deadline September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET
Scholarship decisions September 4, 2026
Geographic eligibility Open globally
Prior climate-science knowledge Not required

About the Climate Education and Community Engagement Course

Climate change is frequently discussed as a scientific and environmental issue, but it is also an educational, social, communication and community-development challenge.

Educators and community practitioners are increasingly expected to help people understand climate change, identify its local effects, respond constructively to climate anxiety and participate in meaningful action.

The Cornell Climate Education and Community Engagement course aims to help learners connect climate knowledge with:

  • Local experience
  • Public communication
  • Education
  • Community participation
  • Youth engagement
  • Climate resilience
  • Adaptation
  • Practical environmental action

Rather than treating climate education as the simple transfer of scientific information, the course explores how educators and practitioners can communicate climate issues constructively and help communities identify realistic opportunities for participation and action.

The course is delivered by the Cornell Civic Ecology Lab with support from researchers, graduate students and teaching assistants associated with Cornell University’s Department of Natural Resources and the Environment.

Full course information is available on the official Climate Education and Community Engagement course page.

Course Dates and Duration

The 2026 course will run from:

September 8 to October 4, 2026

The program lasts four weeks and is delivered online.

Participants should plan to spend approximately four to five hours per week completing the course materials, discussions and activities. The certificate documents 25 professional development hours after the learner completes the required weekly work and final project.

Because the course is conducted over a defined four-week period, prospective participants should ensure that they can participate regularly throughout the program.

Scholarship Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for a need-based scholarship is:

September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time

Scholarship decisions are expected to be announced on:

September 4, 2026

The official page does not publish a separate final registration deadline for fee-paying participants. However, because the course begins on September 8, 2026, interested learners should register as early as possible.

What Participants Will Learn

The course is designed to develop a practical understanding of climate education and community engagement.

Participants will explore how to:

  • Build an accurate foundation in climate literacy
  • Explain climate change clearly to different audiences
  • Connect scientific knowledge with local experience
  • Recognize climate risks affecting local communities
  • Identify community strengths, assets and potential partners
  • Communicate climate issues in constructive and action-oriented ways
  • Address climate anxiety through meaningful learning and participation
  • Understand connections between climate change, equity and public participation
  • Explore climate adaptation and community resilience
  • Support youth agency in climate-related learning
  • Move learners from climate awareness toward practical engagement
  • Design a locally relevant climate-education or community-engagement plan

The course is intended to help participants translate knowledge into educational or community practice rather than simply complete theoretical lessons.

Climate Literacy

Climate literacy involves understanding the essential principles of the climate system and the ways climate change affects individuals, communities, ecosystems and institutions.

Within an educational or community setting, climate literacy also involves the ability to:

  • Interpret climate information
  • Distinguish reliable evidence from misinformation
  • Explain climate change in accessible language
  • Relate global climate patterns to local experiences
  • Understand risk, adaptation and resilience
  • Communicate uncertainty responsibly
  • Identify meaningful responses

Participants will develop a foundation they can use when teaching students, engaging families or working with community groups.

Climate Communication

Climate information can be technically complex, politically sensitive or emotionally difficult. People may also experience fear, helplessness or anxiety when discussing climate impacts.

The course examines how educators and community practitioners can communicate climate change in ways that are:

  • Clear
  • Accurate
  • Understandable
  • Constructive
  • Appropriate for the intended audience
  • Connected with local experience
  • Focused on meaningful action

Participants will practice explaining climate issues to a selected audience, which could include:

  • School students
  • University learners
  • Parents
  • Families
  • Community members
  • NGO participants
  • Volunteers
  • Public stakeholders
  • Local decision-makers

This audience-focused approach helps learners avoid overly general communication and develop messages suited to their professional or community context.

Mapping Local Climate Risks and Community Assets

One important component of the course is the identification of local climate risks, community assets and potential partners.

Climate risks may include:

  • Extreme heat
  • Flooding
  • Drought
  • Water scarcity
  • Wildfires
  • Air pollution
  • Coastal impacts
  • Agricultural disruption
  • Food insecurity
  • Health risks
  • Infrastructure vulnerability
  • Displacement or livelihood challenges

Community assets may include:

  • Schools and universities
  • Local government institutions
  • Community groups
  • Youth organizations
  • NGOs and nonprofit organizations
  • Faith-based groups
  • Health services
  • Local experts
  • Environmental networks
  • Volunteer groups
  • Public spaces
  • Existing climate or sustainability initiatives

By considering both risk and community capacity, participants can design activities that respond to actual local needs while building on existing strengths.

Community Engagement and Public Participation

The course explores climate action as a collaborative process rather than an activity led only by technical experts.

Participants consider how communities can become involved in:

  • Identifying local concerns
  • Sharing lived experiences
  • Discussing climate risks
  • Contributing local knowledge
  • Designing educational programs
  • Participating in adaptation planning
  • Developing resilience strategies
  • Supporting youth participation
  • Building partnerships
  • Taking collective action

This approach recognizes that communities are not simply recipients of climate information. They can also be active contributors to learning, planning and decision-making.

Climate Equity, Adaptation and Resilience

Climate change does not affect every population equally. Communities can differ in their exposure to hazards, access to financial resources, infrastructure, political influence and capacity to recover.

The course connects climate education with questions of:

  • Equity
  • Inclusion
  • Public participation
  • Local vulnerability
  • Adaptation
  • Community capacity
  • Resilience
  • Environmental justice

Participants are encouraged to think about how education and engagement initiatives can respond to diverse community circumstances.

Youth Climate Learning and Agency

Young people are an important audience for climate education. However, teaching climate change only as a global crisis can produce fear or helplessness.

The course explores constructive approaches that help young people:

  • Understand climate change
  • Relate climate issues to their communities
  • Express their concerns
  • Participate in discussions
  • Identify realistic forms of action
  • Build problem-solving skills
  • Develop confidence and agency
  • Work collaboratively with others

Parents, teachers, caregivers and community educators can use these approaches to support informed and meaningful youth participation.

Course Activities

Participants will apply course concepts to a school, organization, community, professional program or project idea of their own.

During the course, learners will:

  1. Study research-informed learning materials.
  2. Watch short instructional videos.
  3. Review climate-education and community-engagement case studies.
  4. Participate in peer discussions.
  5. Identify a climate issue relevant to their local or professional setting.
  6. Select a specific audience for climate communication.
  7. Practice explaining climate change to that audience.
  8. Map local climate risks and community assets.
  9. Identify organizations or individuals who could serve as partners.
  10. Explore strategies for moving from awareness to participation.
  11. Draft a climate-education or community-engagement plan.
  12. Refine the plan using course concepts and peer feedback.
  13. Submit a final project describing the plan and practical next steps.

Final Project

The final project is intended to help participants convert their learning into something useful for their own setting.

Depending on the participant’s role and context, the project may take the form of:

  • A climate-education lesson plan
  • A nature-education lesson
  • A community program activity
  • A youth-engagement initiative
  • A public climate-communication activity
  • A local awareness campaign
  • A climate-resilience learning activity
  • A community-engagement plan
  • An NGO or nonprofit program concept
  • An adaptation-focused educational activity

The final project should outline the learner’s proposed activity, intended audience and practical next steps.

Participants must complete the final project, together with the required weekly work, to qualify for the course certificate.

Online Course Format

The course is primarily asynchronous.

This means participants can generally complete weekly materials at times that suit their schedules rather than attending every class at a fixed time.

Weekly modules may include:

  • Videos
  • Readings
  • Research-informed materials
  • Case studies
  • Discussion prompts
  • Peer exchanges
  • Reflective exercises
  • Practical activities
  • Project-development tasks

The asynchronous structure makes the course accessible across different countries and time zones.

Optional Live Component

An optional live webinar or discussion session will be included.

Participants who cannot attend the live session can access a recording. This is particularly helpful for international participants whose local time zones may make live attendance difficult.

The live session may provide an opportunity to:

  • Discuss course themes
  • Hear from instructors or facilitators
  • Ask questions
  • Exchange experiences
  • Learn from other participants
  • Obtain guidance on practical application

The official page describes the live component as optional, so participants should not assume that inability to attend live will automatically prevent course completion.

Learning Platforms and Technology

The course uses:

  • edX Edge for course modules and discussions
  • Zoom for live sessions

Prospective learners should have:

  • Reliable internet access
  • A computer, tablet or compatible device
  • A working email address
  • The ability to access edX Edge
  • Access to Zoom if they plan to attend live
  • Basic ability to download, complete and upload files
  • Sufficient English proficiency to understand the course materials and participate in discussions

The official course page does not state that advanced technical skills are required.

Social and Applied Learning

The course uses a learning approach based on:

  • Social learning
  • Reflection
  • Practical application
  • Peer exchange
  • Local relevance
  • Case-study analysis

Participants learn by applying course ideas to their own context and sharing examples, resources and feedback with other learners.

The global structure allows participants to compare climate-education and engagement experiences from different communities and countries.

Who Should Take the Course?

The course is designed for a broad global audience.

School, informal and community educators

Teachers and educators can use the course to strengthen their ability to explain climate change and incorporate constructive climate learning into lessons or programs.

NGO and nonprofit professionals

Professionals designing climate, sustainability, youth or community initiatives can use the course to improve their engagement strategies and program planning.

Community leaders and volunteers

Individuals working on local climate action, adaptation, public participation or resilience can learn how to connect community knowledge with educational activities.

University students

Students interested in environmental studies, education, climate change, public policy, development, communication or community engagement can build a practical foundation through the course.

Early-career professionals

The course can help early-career professionals understand how climate education and community participation can be incorporated into professional projects.

Parents and caregivers

Parents, caregivers and family educators can explore practical ways to support climate learning and agency among children and young people.

Environmental education professionals

Experienced professionals can use the program to update existing environmental-education activities with a stronger focus on climate literacy, communication and action.

Eligibility Requirements

The course is open globally.

The official page does not require:

  • A university degree
  • Previous professional experience
  • Previous climate-science training
  • Employment with an environmental organization
  • Citizenship in a particular country
  • Formal teaching qualifications

No prior background in climate science is required.

Participants should, however, be prepared to complete approximately four to five hours of weekly coursework and submit a final project.

Tuition and Tiered Pricing

The Cornell Civic Ecology Lab uses tiered pricing to make the course more accessible to educators and practitioners worldwide.

Standard fee: $90

The standard fee applies to residents of:

  • United States
  • Canada
  • European countries
  • Japan
  • South Korea
  • Singapore
  • Mainland China
  • Taiwan
  • Israel
  • Australia
  • New Zealand

Reduced fee: $20

The reduced fee applies to participants residing in all other countries.

This means residents of many countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East and the Pacific can qualify for the reduced rate.

The fee category is based on the participant’s country of residence rather than citizenship.

Fee for Participants Residing in Pakistan

Participants residing in Pakistan fall within the “all other countries” category and should therefore qualify for the reduced $20 fee.

Pakistani applicants may also seek one of the limited need-based scholarships if they require financial support.

Need-Based Scholarships

A limited number of competitive, need-based scholarships are available.

The official page does not specify:

  • The number of scholarships
  • The exact monetary value
  • Whether every scholarship covers the complete course fee
  • The number of applicants expected
  • A guaranteed award for any particular country or profession

Applicants should therefore understand that financial assistance is limited and competitive.

How to Apply for a Scholarship

Applicants seeking scholarship support should:

  1. Visit the official course page.
  2. Download the 2026 CECE Scholarship Application Word document.
  3. Complete all required sections of the document.
  4. Save the completed document as a PDF.
  5. Open the online course-registration form.
  6. Upload the PDF as part of the registration process.
  7. Submit the registration and scholarship request by September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET.
  8. Wait for the scholarship decision expected on September 4, 2026.

Applicants should complete the scholarship document before beginning the online registration form.

Cornell University Certificate

Participants who complete the course requirements will receive a Cornell University PDF certificate in Climate Education and Community Engagement.

The certificate documents:

25 professional development hours

To receive the certificate, participants must complete:

  • Required weekly coursework
  • Relevant activities and discussions
  • The final project

The certificate is a professional-development credential. The official page does not state that it carries Cornell academic credit, constitutes admission to Cornell University or can be counted toward a Cornell degree.

Participants should not describe themselves as Cornell students or alumni solely on the basis of completing this short online course.

Course Team

The course is offered by the Cornell Civic Ecology Lab with support from researchers, graduate students and teaching assistants.

Fish Yu

Fish Yu is associated with Cornell University’s Department of Natural Resources and the Environment. Yu holds a Master of Science from Cornell University with specialization in public participation and climate governance and has worked with environmental educators and sustainability practitioners internationally.

Professor Marianne Krasny

Professor Marianne Krasny is a scholar in environmental education and civic ecology at Cornell University. She has authored multiple books and research publications, including work informing the course.

Alex Kudryavtsev

Alex Kudryavtsev is a researcher in sustainability education and urban environmental education at Cornell University. His published work includes a framework for nature education.

Hamid Nikzad

Hamid Nikzad is a Cornell graduate student conducting research related to agriculture, human well-being and climate change. He serves as the course administrator and supports participant questions.

How to Register

Interested participants can follow these steps:

  1. Read the complete course information.
  2. Confirm availability from September 8 to October 4, 2026.
  3. Determine whether the standard or reduced fee applies to their country of residence.
  4. Decide whether to request need-based scholarship support.
  5. Download and complete the scholarship document if applying for assistance.
  6. Save the scholarship application as a PDF.
  7. Open the official registration form.
  8. Provide the requested personal and professional information.
  9. Upload the scholarship PDF where applicable.
  10. Submit the form.
  11. Follow any payment or enrolment instructions received from the course team.
  12. Retain a copy of the registration confirmation.

Register for the Climate Education and Community Engagement course

Important Dates

Activity Date
Scholarship application deadline September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET
Scholarship decisions announced September 4, 2026
Course begins September 8, 2026
Course ends October 4, 2026

A separate general registration deadline is not stated on the official course page. Early registration is recommended.

Important Points Before Registering

Prospective participants should remember that:

  • The course is online.
  • It runs for four weeks.
  • Most learning activities are asynchronous.
  • The optional live session will be recorded.
  • edX Edge is used for modules and discussions.
  • Zoom is used for live activities.
  • The anticipated workload is four to five hours per week.
  • No prior climate-science background is required.
  • Participation is open globally.
  • The standard fee is $90.
  • The reduced fee is $20.
  • Scholarships are limited and competitive.
  • The scholarship deadline is September 1, 2026.
  • Certificate eligibility requires completion of weekly work and the final project.
  • The certificate documents 25 professional development hours.
  • The course is not advertised as an academic-credit program.

Contact Information

Questions can be directed to:

Email: CivicEcology@cornell.edu

Applicants should include “CECE” in the email subject line so that the course administrator can identify the inquiry.

Conclusion

The Cornell Climate Education and Community Engagement online course provides an accessible opportunity for learners worldwide to develop practical skills in climate literacy, communication, local risk assessment, community participation, youth agency and climate resilience.

Running from September 8 to October 4, 2026, the course combines asynchronous weekly modules, research-informed materials, short videos, case studies, discussions, practical activities and an optional recorded live session.

Participants will apply their learning to a real school, organization, community or project idea and produce a practical climate-education or engagement plan. Those who complete the weekly requirements and final project will receive a Cornell University PDF certificate documenting 25 professional development hours.

No previous climate-science training or university degree is required. Tiered pricing makes the course more accessible internationally, while a limited number of competitive, need-based scholarships are available to applicants who submit the required document by September 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

item.content:encoded:
The Citadel Conference Travel Grant is an opportunity designed to support promising students in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) who want to attend leading academic and research conferences around the world.

The program is intended to help rising talent participate in conferences where they can present their research, exchange ideas, connect with researchers and industry professionals, and gain exposure to developments at the forefront of their fields.

For selected applicants, Citadel provides substantial financial support covering major conference-related expenses, including the conference registration or full-access pass, round-trip airfare, accommodation, airport transportation, and a food stipend. Recipients may also have opportunities to attend Citadel-hosted dinners and recruitment events during their chosen conference.

The grant is particularly relevant to students pursuing mathematics, computer science, physics, statistics, electrical engineering, and other quantitative disciplines.

What Is the Citadel Conference Travel Grant?

The Citadel Conference Travel Grant is a conference funding initiative created to expand opportunities for exceptional students and emerging STEM researchers.

Academic and research conferences are important platforms for students and researchers to:

  • Present research findings
  • Publish and discuss academic work
  • Exchange ideas with experts
  • Discover new developments in their disciplines
  • Build professional networks
  • Meet potential collaborators
  • Learn about career opportunities
  • Gain exposure to leading organizations and researchers

However, conference attendance can be expensive, particularly for students who need to travel internationally.

The Citadel Conference Travel Grant aims to reduce this financial barrier by providing selected students with comprehensive travel support.

What Does the Citadel Conference Travel Grant Cover?

Selected applicants can receive support for several major expenses associated with attending an eligible conference.

1. Full-Access Conference Pass

Citadel will cover the entire cost of a full-access conference pass for selected applicants.

This allows recipients to participate in the eligible conference without having to personally cover the conference registration cost.

Important: The full-access conference pass benefit does not apply to the Grace Hopper Celebration.

2. Round-Trip Airfare

Citadel will provide round-trip airfare for selected recipients.

This is particularly valuable for students attending international conferences because airfare can represent a significant portion of the total cost of conference participation.

3. Accommodation

Selected students will receive lodging support for the duration of their conference participation.

The accommodation is arranged through Citadel’s designated travel arrangements.

4. Airport and Local Transportation

Recipients will receive travel support for transportation to and from the airport.

Citadel also provides Uber vouchers for transportation during the conference week.

5. Food Stipend

Grant recipients will receive a meal stipend to help cover food expenses during their conference attendance.

Details regarding the food stipend are provided to selected recipients at a later stage.

6. Exclusive Citadel Events

Selected recipients may have the opportunity to participate in Citadel-hosted dinners and recruitment events associated with their chosen conference.

These events can provide students with opportunities to meet Citadel professionals and learn more about careers and work in quantitative and technology-focused fields.

Who Is the Citadel Conference Travel Grant For?

The program is designed for students who are currently pursuing:

  • Bachelor’s degrees
  • Master’s degrees
  • PhD programs

Citadel is particularly interested in applicants studying:

  • Mathematics
  • Computer Science
  • Physics
  • Statistics
  • Electrical Engineering
  • Other quantitative disciplines

Students in related quantitative fields may also be considered.

Preference for Research Conference Applicants

For applicants attending research conferences where papers are published, preference may be given to students who have submitted at least one paper to the conference.

Examples of research-focused conferences include major events such as:

  • ICML
  • NeurIPS
  • ICLR
  • ACL

Submitting a paper does not necessarily mean that every applicant will be selected, but research involvement can strengthen an application where applicable.

What Does Citadel Look For in Applicants?

Selection is based on several factors.

Academic Performance

The selection panel considers the applicant’s academic performance and overall record.

Students with strong academic achievements may be more competitive.

Research and Publication Record

Applicants with research experience and publications may receive favorable consideration.

For conferences that publish academic papers, submitting or presenting research can strengthen an application.

Awards and Previous Achievements

The panel also considers previous awards and other evidence of academic or professional accomplishment.

Applicants should therefore highlight relevant:

  • Academic awards
  • Research awards
  • Competitions
  • Scholarships
  • Publications
  • Research projects
  • Other notable achievements

Presentation and Conference Involvement

Citadel gives priority to applicants who are actively involved in their chosen conference.

This may include:

  • Presenting a research paper
  • Presenting a poster
  • Participating actively in the conference

Applicants who are presenting or otherwise contributing to the academic program can demonstrate a stronger connection between the conference and their research or professional development.

This preference does not apply to the Grace Hopper Celebration.

Potential Impact

The selection panel also considers the potential impact that attending the conference could have on:

  • The applicant’s research
  • Academic development
  • Professional development
  • Future career
  • Citadel’s objectives

Applicants should therefore be able to explain why attending the particular conference is important to their academic or professional goals.

Eligible Conferences

The current conference travel grant program identifies several eligible conferences.

These include:

  1. Grace Hopper Celebration
  2. NeurIPS – Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
  3. Joint March Meeting and April Meeting – Global Physics Summit
  4. ICLR – International Conference on Learning Representations
  5. ICML – International Conference on Machine Learning
  6. ACL – Association for Computational Linguistics

Applicants should check the specific conference requirements and application deadlines because timelines vary from one conference to another.

Upcoming Conference Opportunities

NeurIPS 2026

Conference: NeurIPS – Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems

Location: Sydney, Australia

Conference Dates: December 6–12, 2026

Application Deadline: October 5, 2026

Applicant Notification: October 9, 2026

NeurIPS is a major international conference focused on machine learning, artificial intelligence, and related areas.

Students whose research aligns with machine learning, AI, statistics, computer science, and related quantitative disciplines may find this conference particularly relevant.

Grace Hopper Celebration 2026

Location: Anaheim, California, USA

Conference Dates: October 27–30, 2026

Application Deadline: September 25, 2026

Applicant Notification: October 5, 2026

The Grace Hopper Celebration is one of the major conferences associated with women in computing and technology.

Applicants interested in attending this conference should note that it has specific grant arrangements and requirements.

Most importantly, the standard full-access conference pass coverage described for other eligible conferences does not apply to the Grace Hopper Celebration.

Applicants should therefore carefully review the conference-specific terms before applying.

Important Deadlines at a Glance

Because the Citadel Conference Travel Grant supports multiple conferences, there is not one universal application deadline.

Applicants must follow the deadline associated with the specific conference they wish to attend.

NeurIPS 2026

Application Deadline: October 5, 2026

Notification: October 9, 2026

Grace Hopper Celebration 2026

Application Deadline: September 25, 2026

Notification: October 5, 2026

Applicants interested in other eligible conferences should consult the Citadel Conference Travel Grant page for the applicable conference-specific timeline.

How the Grant Is Delivered

Selected applicants do not simply receive a lump-sum travel payment.

Citadel manages many of the travel arrangements directly.

The process generally includes:

  • Citadel purchasing the conference pass directly
  • Flights being arranged through Citadel’s travel agency
  • Hotel accommodation being booked through the travel agency
  • Uber vouchers being provided for airport and local transportation
  • Food stipend information being provided to recipients

This approach helps selected students focus on participating in the conference rather than managing the major travel expenses themselves.

Must Applicants Attend in Person?

Yes.

Selected applicants are expected to attend the conference in person.

Students who are only presenting remotely or participating virtually are not eligible for the travel grant on that basis.

The purpose of the grant is to facilitate physical participation at eligible conferences and enable recipients to benefit from direct networking, presentations, discussions, and professional engagement.

Can Students Apply for Multiple Conferences?

Yes.

Students may apply for the Citadel Conference Travel Grant for multiple conferences within the same year.

There is no stated limit on the number of conference travel grants an applicant can apply for.

However, applicants should ensure that they meet the eligibility and conference-specific requirements for every application they submit.

Are There Post-Conference Requirements?

No.

Selected recipients do not have to provide a report or presentation after attending the conference.

There are no post-conference obligations specified for successful grant recipients.

How to Strengthen Your Application

Students interested in this opportunity should prepare a strong application that clearly demonstrates their academic and professional potential.

Consider highlighting:

Academic Excellence

Include relevant academic achievements and demonstrate your strength in your field of study.

Research Experience

Explain your current research interests, projects, publications, or other research activities.

Conference Participation

If applicable, clearly state whether you will:

  • Present a paper
  • Present a poster
  • Participate in a research session
  • Contribute to the conference in another meaningful way

Publications

If you have published academic research, make sure relevant publications are clearly presented.

Awards

Include significant academic, research, technology, or professional awards.

Conference Relevance

Explain why attending the specific conference is important to your work and how participation could contribute to your academic or professional development.

Why the Citadel Conference Travel Grant Matters

For students, attending an international research conference can be a transformative academic and professional experience.

A conference can provide opportunities to:

  • Learn from leading researchers
  • Discover emerging developments
  • Receive feedback on research
  • Meet potential collaborators
  • Build an international professional network
  • Explore career opportunities
  • Gain confidence presenting research
  • Understand current challenges within a discipline

The cost of international conference participation, however, can prevent many talented students from attending.

By covering major travel and participation expenses, the Citadel Conference Travel Grant helps reduce this barrier and gives selected students the opportunity to participate in leading conferences.

Conclusion

The Citadel Conference Travel Grant offers an excellent opportunity for ambitious STEM students to participate in leading academic and research conferences without having to personally shoulder the major costs of international conference travel.

Through support for conference passes, flights, accommodation, transportation, and meals, the program enables students to focus on research, learning, networking, and professional development.

The opportunity is particularly valuable for students in mathematics, computer science, physics, statistics, electrical engineering, and other quantitative disciplines, especially those with strong academic records, research experience, publications, awards, or active involvement in conferences.

Students should carefully review the conference-specific requirements and deadlines. For the currently listed 2026 opportunities, the Grace Hopper Celebration deadline is September 25, 2026, while the NeurIPS deadline is October 5, 2026.
